vignette:
Hassan is a 55-year-old farmer who lives with his wife and adult son on a small olive and wheat farm in a rural valley. He came to therapy reluctantly, sent by his son, who told him he has not been himself for two years. Hassan sits in the chair with his hands on his knees, looking at the floor. He speaks slowly, as if he is describing someone else’s life.

The attack happened during the olive harvest two Octobers ago. Hassan was working alone in the far grove, the one his father planted. He heard a truck pull up—strange for that hour. Two men got out. They asked for directions, then one grabbed him from behind while the other hit him across the jaw with a metal pipe. They took his wallet, his phone, and the cash he had in the truck for paying seasonal workers. They left him bleeding among the trees. He lay there for three hours before his son found him.

In the weeks that followed, Hassan stayed home. He told himself he was healing from the concussion, that the bruises needed time. But he did not go back to the grove. When his son asked him to help with pruning, he said his back hurt. He started waking at 3 a.m. drenched in sweat, the sound of metal hitting bone ringing in his ears. In the dream, the men are always just out of reach, and he cannot run because his legs will not move.

Now, two years later, Hassan works but avoids the far section of the farm entirely. He has paved a new path that lets him drive around it, adding twenty minutes to his daily rounds. His son does the pruning in that grove, and Hassan feels a hot, acidic guilt every time he sees him go. He tells himself he is being foolish, that the men are long gone, but his body does not listen. His heart pounds whenever a vehicle approaches the gate. He checks the padlock three times before bed.

At home, his wife complains that he is jumpy and short-tempered. He snapped at her last week for putting salt in his soup instead of pepper, then spent the evening in the barn with the tractor, not speaking. He feels disconnected from his family, as if a pane of glass has slid down between him and everyone he loves. His son tries to joke with him, but Hassan cannot laugh. He cannot remember the last time he felt any pleasure—not from the taste of bread, not from the sight of the hills in the morning, not from the warmth of the sun.

He has not told anyone that he carries a heavy wrench in his jacket pocket whenever he leaves the house. He does not know if he would use it. He only knows that without it, the anxiety spikes so high he has to pull over and breathe into his hands. He has started drinking a glass of arak every evening, then two. His wife does not know.

Last month, Hassan’s son found him standing at the edge of the far grove for fifteen minutes, staring at the trees. He was not crying. He was just… empty. When his son asked what he was doing, Hassan said he was trying to remember what it felt like to not be scared. He could not find the memory.
